overview: Rupert’s Land was the Hudson’s Bay Company’s claimed trading territory in the Hudson Bay watershed, established by an English charter in 1670. Indigenous nations lived and governed there. The map’s 1783 to 1815 slice is shorter than the company jurisdiction’s history. Its imported outline extends beyond that watershed and remains unverified.

periods.title: Charter and competing traders
periods.summary: A royal charter supported company trading claims; posts depended on Indigenous knowledge and exchange.

periods.title: Company consolidation and resistance
periods.summary: After the fur companies merged, a more rigid hierarchy restricted many locally born employees.

items.text: A “made beaver” was a unit of value based on one prime beaver skin. Traders could reckon an exchange in beavers without handing over a tidy stack of coins. The fur trade had its own accounting vocabulary.

York boats moved freight inland using a square sail and oars. The largest reached about 40 feet long and could carry more than seventy-five packs averaging forty kilograms each. Eight oarsmen supplied the engine when wind would not cooperate.

Thanadelthur, a Dene interpreter, helped bring Dene and Cree negotiators to a peace agreement in 1715 to 1716. She spoke several languages and completed the expedition’s final leg herself after illness and hunger stopped others. Trade routes were also diplomatic achievements.

Many European traders and Indigenous women formed lasting marriages recognized through local custom. Some couples later held Christian ceremonies, with several children baptized together. The records reveal families spanning cultures, rather than a trading world populated only by solitary men.

Indigenous women hunted, trapped, fished and prepared food. Their work helped sustain trade communities. In the nineteenth century, increasingly racist colonial social rules could exclude these women from circles that had previously accepted their families.

Small company schools opened at Moose Factory, Eastmain, York and Churchill in 1794. Some locally born sons also entered apprenticeships. After the 1821 merger, however, company hierarchies increasingly blocked their promotion: education did not guarantee equal treatment.

sections.title: An uncomfortable building and useful rubbish

items.text: At York Factory, archaeologists found an older star-shaped fort beneath the later warehouse. Built in 1788 to 1795, the “Octagon” combined accommodation and storage around a courtyard. Its remains survived beneath the depot constructed during the 1830s.

The Octagon’s heavy foundations proved poorly suited to ground that froze and heaved. Brick, stone and rigid walls cracked under that movement. A building design that behaved well in Britain had encountered a very different landlord: permafrost.

Excavators recovered a thick ring of household rubbish around the fort, probably tossed from windows. They also found cellars, chimney remains and a possible oven from the 1810 cookroom. Yesterday’s untidy habits became tomorrow’s archaeological evidence.

sections.title: Writing and the transfer to Canada

items.text: A short Latin sample is the company motto “Pro pelle cutem”: “skin for skin.” Historian E. E. Rich identifies prints of the arms and motto dating to 1679. Its deeper joke or intended message remains debated; the wording itself is securely attested.

When Canada sought control, the Red River Métis resisted and established a provisional government. Negotiations helped produce the Manitoba Act of 1870. The Métis community participated as a negotiating partner in creating Manitoba, rather than simply receiving a new ruler.

The Manitoba Act promised 1.4 million acres for Métis children. Canada did not implement that commitment diligently; a 2013 Supreme Court decision recognized the failure. The territorial transfer therefore left a major legacy of unresolved land rights.

ending.text: The company jurisdiction was incorporated into Canada in 1870, following the 1869 surrender agreement. The map endpoint of 1815 is not its ending. Indigenous and Métis peoples continued their own communities and struggles over land and government.
